import FormalConjecturesUtil
import FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks for an algorithm that recognizes the unknot, given a finite
representation of a knot. It is decidable (Haken, 1961), it lies in `NP` (Hass, Lagarias and
Pippenger, 1999) and in `co-NP` (Lackenby, 2016). Whether it lies in `P`, that is, whether
unknots can be recognized in polynomial time, is open.

Following Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, a knot is a simple closed polygon in `ℝ³`, represented by
the cyclic list of its vertices, which have integer coordinates. The input length is the number of
bits needed to write these coordinates in binary. This representation is polynomial-time
equivalent to knot diagrams (with the crossing number as size), so the choice of representation
does not affect the question. As in Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, the decision problem is
formulated as a language: an input is accepted if and only if it is a knot and this knot is
trivial.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- J. Hass, J. C. Lagarias, N. Pippenger, *The computational complexity of knot and link problems*,
  J. ACM 46 (1999), 185–211. [arXiv:math/9807016](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- M. Lackenby, *The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm*,
  Adv. Math. 387 (2021). [arXiv:1604.00290](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/
open Computability
namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- Euclidean three-space. -/

/- ### Polygonal knots -/

/-- The point of `ℝ³` with integer coordinates `p 0`, `p 1`, `p 2`. -/
def toPoint (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : ℝ³ := WithLp.toLp 2 fun i => (p i : ℝ)

blocks.code:
noncomputable def loop (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) (x : Fin v.length × ℝ) : ℝ³ :=
  (1 - x.2) • toPoint v[x.1] + x.2 • toPoint v[finRotate v.length x.1]
blocks.docstring:
The piecewise-linear parametrisation of the closed polygon with vertex list `v`.
The parameter `(k, t)` is sent to the point at fraction `t` along the `k`-th edge, which joins the
vertex `v[k]` to the cyclically next vertex `v[finRotate v.length k]` (`finRotate` is the cyclic
shift `k ↦ k + 1` of `Fin v.length`, so the last edge joins the last vertex to the first).

justification.closest_existing_considered: `segment ℝ a b` (used in the API lemma); `Path`/`Homotopy` are not suitable for a finite combinatorial input.
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.toPoint / loop / polygon
justification.why_needed: Mathlib has no knot theory; these realize a list of integer vertices as a piecewise-linear closed curve in ℝ³ (polygon = union of the edge segments, proved as `polygon_eq_iUnion_segment`).

blocks.name: loop
blocks.text:
/-- The piecewise-linear parametrisation of the closed polygon with vertex list `v`.
The parameter `(k, t)` is sent to the point at fraction `t` along the `k`-th edge, which joins the
vertex `v[k]` to the cyclically next vertex `v[finRotate v.length k]` (`finRotate` is the cyclic
shift `k ↦ k + 1` of `Fin v.length`, so the last edge joins the last vertex to the first). -/
noncomputable def loop (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) (x : Fin v.length × ℝ) : ℝ³ :=
  (1 - x.2) • toPoint v[x.1] + x.2 • toPoint v[finRotate v.length x.1]

blocks.code:
noncomputable def polygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  loop v '' (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Icc 0 1)
blocks.docstring:
The closed polygon with vertex list `v`, as a subset of `ℝ³`: the union of the segments
joining cyclically consecutive vertices (see `polygon_eq_iUnion_segment`).

justification.closest_existing_considered: `segment ℝ a b` (used in the API lemma); `Path`/`Homotopy` are not suitable for a finite combinatorial input.

/-- The closed polygon with vertex list `v`, as a subset of `ℝ³`: the union of the segments
joining cyclically consecutive vertices (see `polygon_eq_iUnion_segment`). -/
noncomputable def polygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  loop v '' (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Icc 0 1)

blocks.code:
def IsPolygonalKnot (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Prop :=
  3 ≤ v.length ∧ Set.InjOn (loop v) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Ico 0 1)
blocks.docstring:
The vertex list `v` is a *polygonal knot*: it has at least three vertices and the closed
polygon through them is simple, i.e. its parametrisation `loop v` is injective on one period
`Fin v.length × [0, 1)`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Set.InjOn` (used); no notion of simple polygon or PL embedding exists in Mathlib.
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.IsPolygonalKnot
justification.why_needed: Simplicity of the closed polygon (HLP's definition of a PL knot), expressed as injectivity of the parametrisation on one period.

blocks.name: IsPolygonalKnot
blocks.text:
/-- The vertex list `v` is a *polygonal knot*: it has at least three vertices and the closed
polygon through them is simple, i.e. its parametrisation `loop v` is injective on one period
`Fin v.length × [0, 1)`. -/
def IsPolygonalKnot (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Prop :=
  3 ≤ v.length ∧ Set.InjOn (loop v) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Ico 0 1)

blocks.code: def standardCircle : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}
blocks.docstring: The standard unknot: the unit circle in the `xy`-plane.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Homeomorph` (used); Mathlib has no knot equivalence, isotopy or Reidemeister moves.
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.standardCircle / IsUnknot
justification.why_needed: The unknot: a subset of ℝ³ carried onto the unit circle in the xy-plane by a homeomorphism of ℝ³.

blocks.name: standardCircle
blocks.text:
/-- The standard unknot: the unit circle in the `xy`-plane. -/
def standardCircle : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}

blocks.code: def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle
blocks.docstring:
A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an *unknot* (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it
onto the standard circle. The homeomorphism is not required to preserve orientation: the
standard circle is preserved by the reflection `p 2 ↦ -p 2`, so this is the same as asking for
an orientation preserving homeomorphism, or for an ambient isotopy. For polygonal knots this is
equivalent (by Dehn's lemma) to the piecewise-linear notion used by Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger:
the knot can be deformed, through simple polygons, to a planar polygon.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Homeomorph` (used); Mathlib has no knot equivalence, isotopy or Reidemeister moves.
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.standardCircle / IsUnknot
justification.why_needed: The unknot: a subset of ℝ³ carried onto the unit circle in the xy-plane by a homeomorphism of ℝ³.

blocks.name: IsUnknot
blocks.text:
/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an *unknot* (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it
onto the standard circle. The homeomorphism is not required to preserve orientation: the
standard circle is preserved by the reflection `p 2 ↦ -p 2`, so this is the same as asking for
an orientation preserving homeomorphism, or for an ambient isotopy. For polygonal knots this is
equivalent (by Dehn's lemma) to the piecewise-linear notion used by Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger:
the knot can be deformed, through simple polygons, to a planar polygon. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle

blocks.code:
noncomputable def isUnknottedPolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Bool :=
  decide (IsPolygonalKnot v ∧ IsUnknot (polygon v))
blocks.docstring:
Unknot recognition as a Boolean function on vertex lists: `isUnknottedPolygon v = true` if and
only if `v` is a polygonal knot and this knot is trivial. Vertex lists that do not describe a knot
are rejected.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `ComplexityTheory.DecisionProblem` / `ComplexityTheory.P` from PvsNP.lean (reused as the type and the class).
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.isUnknottedPolygon / unknotLanguage
justification.why_needed: The decision problem as a Boolean function on vertex lists and as a language over `Bool` fitting `ComplexityTheory.P`.

open scoped Classical in
/-- Unknot recognition as a Boolean function on vertex lists: `isUnknottedPolygon v = true` if and

are rejected. -/
noncomputable def isUnknottedPolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Bool :=

/- ### Encoding of polygonal representations

A vertex list is written as a word over a four-letter alphabet: the three coordinates of a vertex
are written in binary and separated by commas, and consecutive vertices are separated by
semicolons. Each letter is then written as two bits. The length of the resulting bit string is,
up to a constant factor, the number of bits of the coordinates: the input length of Hass, Lagarias
and Pippenger. -/

blocks.code:
inductive Alphabet
  | digit (b : Bool)
  | comma
  | semicolon
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype
blocks.docstring:
The input alphabet: binary digits, a separator between the coordinates of a vertex and a
separator between consecutive vertices.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Computability.FinEncoding`, `finEncodingNatBool`, `finEncodingListBool`, `Encodable`/`Denumerable ℤ` (the latter used for the ℤ↔ℕ zigzag), `Nat.digits`/`Nat.ofDigits` (used).
justification.name: UnknottingProblem.Alphabet, Alphabet.toBits/ofBits, encodeInt/decodeInt, encodeVertex/decodeVertex, encodeVertices/decodeVertices, polygonEncoding
justification.why_needed: A polynomial-size binary `FinEncoding` of vertex lists; Mathlib has no list/product encodings of polynomial size (its `Encodable` list encoding via `Nat.pair` is exponential) and the repo only has `finEncodingListBool`/`finEncodingListBoolProdListBool`.

def Alphabet.ofBits : List Bool → Option (List Alphabet)
  | [] => some []
  | [_] => none
  | false :: b :: s => (digit b :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: false :: s => (comma :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: true :: s => (semicolon :: ·) <$> ofBits s

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma decodeInt_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : decodeInt (encodeInt z) = z := by
  have h : ∀ d ∈ Nat.digits 2 (Encodable.encode z),
      (if Alphabet.digit (d == 1) = .digit true then 1 else 0) = d := by
    intro d hd
    have := Nat.digits_lt_base (by norm_num) hd
    interval_cases d <;> simp
  simp only [decodeInt, encodeInt, List.map_map, Function.comp_def]
  rw [List.map_congr_left h, List.map_id', Nat.ofDigits_digits, Denumerable.ofNat_encode]

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no question: is the decision problem 'given a (finite, e.g. knot-diagram) representation of a knot, is it the unknot?' in the class P (deterministic polynomial time in input size, e.g. crossing number); the choice of encoding is implicit but any standard one (diagram, PL knot, triangulation of the complement) is polynomially equivalent, and since P is closed under complement it does not matter whether unknottedness or knottedness is the accepted language; the known NP and co-NP memberships and the announced quasi-polynomial algorithm are background, not questions posed by the statement.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates compile and state the same yes/no proposition `answer(sorry) ↔ (unknot language) ∈ P`, differing only in the finite knot representation. c07 is the most rigorous and closest to the primary literature: the instance is exactly Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger's polygonal representation (integer vertex list, simplicity enforced by an explicit injectivity condition `IsPolygonalKnot`, input length = binary size of the coordinates via a `FinEncoding` whose `decode_encode` is proved), unknottedness is the textbook ambient-homeomorphism condition `∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle` (correct for polygonal knots: unknot ⇒ ambient isotopy ⇒ homeomorphism; homeomorphism ⇒ π₁ of complement ≅ ℤ ⇒ trivial by Dehn's lemma; orientation is irrelevant because the round circle is reflection-invariant), and polynomial time is the repository's own `ComplexityTheory.P` (Mathlib TM2, polynomial in the input length). answer(True) = 'yes, unknots can be recognized in polynomial time'. I only added a sentence to the `IsUnknot` docstring explaining why orientation preservation is not required. c02/c08 are equivalent but do not demand simplicity of the polygon explicitly (harmless up to polynomial-time equivalence, but less literal); c01 restricts to nonnegative coordinates and uses `Fin 3 → ℝ`; c03/c04 use the cubic-lattice representation (also mentioned by HLP, fine but less standard); c05 uses a promise formulation with unproven sorry'd test lemmas; c06 defines the unknot indirectly via Markov equivalence of braid words (correct by Markov's theorem, but one step removed from the definition of the unknot).

import FormalConjecturesUtil
import FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP

/-!
# Unknotting problem

The unknotting problem asks for an algorithm that recognizes the unknot, given a finite
representation of a knot. It is decidable (Haken, 1961), it lies in `NP` (Hass, Lagarias and
Pippenger, 1999) and in `co-NP` (Lackenby, 2016). Whether it lies in `P`, that is, whether
unknots can be recognized in polynomial time, is open.

Following Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, a knot is a simple closed polygon in `ℝ³`, represented by
the cyclic list of its vertices, which have integer coordinates. The input length is the number of
bits needed to write these coordinates in binary. This representation is polynomial-time
equivalent to knot diagrams (with the crossing number as size), so the choice of representation
does not affect the question. As in Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, the decision problem is
formulated as a language: an input is accepted if and only if it is a knot and this knot is
trivial.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Unknotting problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unknotting_problem)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- J. Hass, J. C. Lagarias, N. Pippenger, *The computational complexity of knot and link problems*,
  J. ACM 46 (1999), 185–211. [arXiv:math/9807016](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9807016)
- M. Lackenby, *The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm*,
  Adv. Math. 387 (2021). [arXiv:1604.00290](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.00290)
-/

open Computability

namespace UnknottingProblem

/-- Euclidean three-space. -/
local notation "ℝ³" => EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)

/- ### Polygonal knots -/

/-- The point of `ℝ³` with integer coordinates `p 0`, `p 1`, `p 2`. -/
def toPoint (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : ℝ³ := WithLp.toLp 2 fun i => (p i : ℝ)

/-- The piecewise-linear parametrisation of the closed polygon with vertex list `v`.
The parameter `(k, t)` is sent to the point at fraction `t` along the `k`-th edge, which joins the
vertex `v[k]` to the cyclically next vertex `v[finRotate v.length k]` (`finRotate` is the cyclic
shift `k ↦ k + 1` of `Fin v.length`, so the last edge joins the last vertex to the first). -/
noncomputable def loop (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) (x : Fin v.length × ℝ) : ℝ³ :=
  (1 - x.2) • toPoint v[x.1] + x.2 • toPoint v[finRotate v.length x.1]

/-- The closed polygon with vertex list `v`, as a subset of `ℝ³`: the union of the segments
joining cyclically consecutive vertices (see `polygon_eq_iUnion_segment`). -/
noncomputable def polygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Set ℝ³ :=
  loop v '' (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Icc 0 1)

/-- The vertex list `v` is a *polygonal knot*: it has at least three vertices and the closed
polygon through them is simple, i.e. its parametrisation `loop v` is injective on one period
`Fin v.length × [0, 1)`. -/
def IsPolygonalKnot (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Prop :=
  3 ≤ v.length ∧ Set.InjOn (loop v) (Set.univ ×ˢ Set.Ico 0 1)

/-- The standard unknot: the unit circle in the `xy`-plane. -/
def standardCircle : Set ℝ³ := {p | p 0 ^ 2 + p 1 ^ 2 = 1 ∧ p 2 = 0}

/-- A subset `K` of `ℝ³` is an *unknot* (a trivial knot) if some homeomorphism of `ℝ³` maps it
onto the standard circle. The homeomorphism is not required to preserve orientation: the
standard circle is preserved by the reflection `p 2 ↦ -p 2`, so this is the same as asking for
an orientation preserving homeomorphism, or for an ambient isotopy. For polygonal knots this is
equivalent (by Dehn's lemma) to the piecewise-linear notion used by Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger:
the knot can be deformed, through simple polygons, to a planar polygon. -/
def IsUnknot (K : Set ℝ³) : Prop := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle

open scoped Classical in
/-- Unknot recognition as a Boolean function on vertex lists: `isUnknottedPolygon v = true` if and
only if `v` is a polygonal knot and this knot is trivial. Vertex lists that do not describe a knot
are rejected. -/
noncomputable def isUnknottedPolygon (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : Bool :=
  decide (IsPolygonalKnot v ∧ IsUnknot (polygon v))

@[category API, AMS 57]
lemma polygon_eq_iUnion_segment (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :
    polygon v =
      ⋃ k : Fin v.length, segment ℝ (toPoint v[k]) (toPoint v[finRotate v.length k]) := by
  ext p
  simp [polygon, loop, segment_eq_image]

@[category test, AMS 57]
lemma polygon_nil : polygon [] = ∅ := by
  simp [polygon, Set.eq_empty_of_isEmpty]

@[category test, AMS 57]
lemma not_isPolygonalKnot_nil : ¬ IsPolygonalKnot [] := by
  simp [IsPolygonalKnot]

@[category test, AMS 57]

  rintro ⟨h, hh⟩
  have : (WithLp.toLp 2 ![1, 0, 0] : ℝ³) ∈ standardCircle := by simp [standardCircle]
  rw [← hh] at this
  simp at this

lemma isUnknottedPolygon_nil : isUnknottedPolygon [] = false := by
  simp [isUnknottedPolygon, IsPolygonalKnot]

/- ### Encoding of polygonal representations

A vertex list is written as a word over a four-letter alphabet: the three coordinates of a vertex
are written in binary and separated by commas, and consecutive vertices are separated by
semicolons. Each letter is then written as two bits. The length of the resulting bit string is,
up to a constant factor, the number of bits of the coordinates: the input length of Hass, Lagarias
and Pippenger. -/

/-- The input alphabet: binary digits, a separator between the coordinates of a vertex and a
separator between consecutive vertices. -/
inductive Alphabet
  | digit (b : Bool)
  | comma
  | semicolon
  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype

/-- Each letter is written as two bits. -/
def Alphabet.toBits : Alphabet → List Bool
  | digit b => [false, b]
  | comma => [true, false]
  | semicolon => [true, true]

/-- Inverse of `List.flatMap Alphabet.toBits`. -/
def Alphabet.ofBits : List Bool → Option (List Alphabet)
  | [] => some []
  | [_] => none
  | false :: b :: s => (digit b :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: false :: s => (comma :: ·) <$> ofBits s
  | true :: true :: s => (semicolon :: ·) <$> ofBits s

/-- The binary expansion (least significant digit first) of the natural number
`Encodable.encode z`, where `Encodable.encode : ℤ → ℕ` is the bijection `n ↦ 2n`,
`-(n + 1) ↦ 2n + 1`. -/
def encodeInt (z : ℤ) : List Alphabet :=
  (Nat.digits 2 (Encodable.encode z)).map fun d => .digit (d == 1)

/-- Inverse of `encodeInt`. -/
def decodeInt (l : List Alphabet) : ℤ :=
  Denumerable.ofNat ℤ (Nat.ofDigits 2 (l.map fun s => if s = .digit true then 1 else 0))

/-- The three coordinates of a vertex, separated by commas. -/
def encodeVertex (p : Fin 3 → ℤ) : List Alphabet :=
  [.comma].intercalate ((List.ofFn p).map encodeInt)

/-- Inverse of `encodeVertex`. -/
def decodeVertex (l : List Alphabet) : Option (Fin 3 → ℤ) :=
  match l.splitOn .comma with
  | [a, b, c] => some ![decodeInt a, decodeInt b, decodeInt c]
  | _ => none

/-- The vertices, separated by semicolons. -/
def encodeVertices (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) : List Alphabet :=
  [.semicolon].intercalate (v.map encodeVertex)

/-- Inverse of `encodeVertices`. -/
def decodeVertices (l : List Alphabet) : Option (List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :=
  match l.splitOn .semicolon with
  | [[]] => some []
  | parts => parts.mapM decodeVertex

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma Alphabet.ofBits_flatMap_toBits (l : List Alphabet) :
    Alphabet.ofBits (l.flatMap Alphabet.toBits) = some l := by
  induction l with
  | nil => rfl
  | cons a l ih => cases a <;> simp [Alphabet.toBits, Alphabet.ofBits, ih]

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma decodeInt_encodeInt (z : ℤ) : decodeInt (encodeInt z) = z := by
  have h : ∀ d ∈ Nat.digits 2 (Encodable.encode z),
      (if Alphabet.digit (d == 1) = .digit true then 1 else 0) = d := by
    intro d hd
    have := Nat.digits_lt_base (by norm_num) hd
    interval_cases d <;> simp
  simp only [decodeInt, encodeInt, List.map_map, Function.comp_def]
  rw [List.map_congr_left h, List.map_id', Nat.ofDigits_digits, Denumerable.ofNat_encode]

/-- The binary encoding of polygonal representations: the vertex list is written as a word over

def polygonEncoding : FinEncoding (List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) where
  Γ := Bool
  encode v := (encodeVertices v).flatMap Alphabet.toBits
  decode s := (Alphabet.ofBits s).bind decodeVertices
  decode_encode v := by simp [Alphabet.ofBits_flatMap_toBits, decodeVertices_encodeVertices]
  ΓFin := inferInstance

@[category test, AMS 68]
lemma polygonEncoding_encode_example :
    polygonEncoding.encode [![0, 0, 0], ![3, -1, 2]] =
      [true, false, true, false, true, true, false, false, false, true, false, true, true, false,
        false, true, true, false, false, false, false, false, false, true] := by
  simp [polygonEncoding, encodeVertices, encodeVertex, encodeInt, List.intercalate, List.ofFn_succ,
    Alphabet.toBits, show Encodable.encode (0 : ℤ) = 0 from rfl,
    show Encodable.encode (3 : ℤ) = 6 from rfl, show Encodable.encode (-1 : ℤ) = 1 from rfl,
    show Encodable.encode (2 : ℤ) = 4 from rfl]

/- ### The problem -/

/-- The unknotting problem as a language over `Bool`: a bit string is accepted if and only if it
decodes (`polygonEncoding.decode`) to a vertex list which is a polygonal knot that is trivial.
Bit strings that do not decode to a vertex list are rejected. -/
noncomputable def unknotLanguage : ComplexityTheory.DecisionProblem := fun s =>
  match polygonEncoding.decode s with
  | some v => isUnknottedPolygon v
  | none => false

@[category API, AMS 68]
lemma unknotLanguage_encode (v : List (Fin 3 → ℤ)) :
    unknotLanguage (polygonEncoding.encode v) = isUnknottedPolygon v := by
  simp [unknotLanguage, polygonEncoding.decode_encode]

/--
**Unknotting problem.** Can unknots be recognized in polynomial time?

Precisely: is there a deterministic Turing machine which, given the binary encoding of a list of
vertices with integer coordinates, decides whether it is a polygonal knot that is trivial, in a
number of steps bounded by a polynomial in the length of the input? That is, does the unknotting
problem `unknotLanguage` lie in the complexity class `P`?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 57 68]
theorem unknotting_problem : answer(sorry) ↔ unknotLanguage ∈ ComplexityTheory.P := by
  sorry

end UnknottingProblem

items: Knot representation: following Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger (arXiv:math/9807016, §1, the primary source for the complexity formulation), a knot is a simple closed polygon in ℝ³ given by the cyclic list of its vertices with integer coordinates; input length = bits of the coordinates in binary. HLP prove this is polynomial-time equivalent to knot diagrams (crossing number as size), so membership in P is representation-independent, as the decomposition notes anticipate.

Decision problem as a language (HLP: 'Instance: a link diagram D. Question: is D a knot diagram that represents the trivial knot?'): `unknotLanguage s = true` iff `s` decodes to a vertex list `v` with `IsPolygonalKnot v ∧ IsUnknot (polygon v)`; non-knot inputs and undecodable strings are rejected. Validity checking is itself polynomial, so this is in P iff the promise version is.

Complexity notion: the repository's `ComplexityTheory.P` from `FormalConjectures.Millenium.PvsNP` (imported, following precedent such as ArtinPrimitiveRootsConjecture importing RiemannHypothesis). P = languages over `List Bool` computable by a deterministic Mathlib TM2 in time polynomial in input length.

Unknot: `IsUnknot K := ∃ h : ℝ³ ≃ₜ ℝ³, h '' K = standardCircle` (Armstrong's textbook definition). For polygonal (tame) knots this agrees with HLP's PL notion: a PL-trivial knot is carried to the round circle by a homeomorphism; conversely such a homeomorphism gives π₁(ℝ³∖K) ≅ ℤ, so K is trivial by Dehn's lemma. Orientation-preservation is not required since the round circle is preserved by a reflection; ℝ³ rather than S³ is used, which is equivalent.

Simplicity: `IsPolygonalKnot v := 3 ≤ v.length ∧ InjOn (loop v) (univ ×ˢ Ico 0 1)` where `loop v (k,t)` is the PL parametrisation of edge k (from `v[k]` to `v[finRotate v.length k]`, the cyclic successor). Injectivity on one period is exactly 'simple closed polygon'; zero-length edges, backtracking and self-intersections are excluded; straight-angle (collinear) vertices are allowed, as they do not change the curve. The condition 3 ≤ length only rules out the vacuous empty list.

Encoding: coordinates written in binary (little-endian) of the zigzag bijection `Encodable.encode : ℤ → ℕ`, separated by commas, vertices separated by semicolons, each of the 4 letters packed into 2 bits. Length is linear in HLP's input length (unlike Mathlib's `Encodable` for lists, which is exponential and was deliberately avoided). `decode_encode` is proved (so `polygonEncoding : FinEncoding`), and a concrete example test confirms the bit pattern.
Ambient space is `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 3)`; the standard unknot is the unit circle in the xy-plane.
